title: The Oscar Voting Body Just Got a Lot More Indian — and It's About Time
excerpt: Vishal Bhardwaj, the editor behind RRR, a Disney animation chief, and four more Indian names join the Academy's 2026 class — putting Indian cinema closer to the ballot than ever before.
body:
The email that changes your relationship with the Oscars forever landed in at least seven Indian inboxes this week.

On Wednesday, the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences unveiled its 2026 class of invitees — 529 artists and executives from across the globe, handpicked to join the body that votes on cinema's most coveted gold statue. Tucked into a list alongside Jacob Elordi, Jenna Ortega, Simu Liu, and the Safdie brothers were names that tell a very different, quietly thrilling story about where Indian cinema stands in the world right now.

Vishal Bhardwaj leads the Indian contingent, invited under the music composition branch. The man who turned Shakespeare into Mumbai noir — *Maqbool*, *Omkara*, *Haider* — and composed some of the most hauntingly beautiful scores in Hindi cinema (go revisit *Maachis* if you've forgotten) now gets a vote in the room that decides Best Picture. Let that land for a second.

But Bhardwaj isn't the only Indian name worth lingering on.

The Invisible Architects

A. Sreekar Prasad — a name most moviegoers wouldn't recognise, and that's precisely the point. Over a 45-year career, Prasad has edited more than 600 films across 17 languages. He cut *Kaminey*. He cut *Talvar*. He worked on *RRR*, the film that stormed the global stage at the 95th Oscars. If Indian cinema has a rhythm, this man built half of it.

Beside him is Deepa Bhatia, the editor whose fingerprints are on some of Bollywood's most emotionally precise work — *Taare Zameen Par*, *My Name Is Khan*, *Rock On!*, *Kai Po Che!*. These are films that didn't just entertain; they recalibrated how mainstream Hindi cinema could feel.

The Craft Behind the Glamour

Eka Lakhani joins as a costume designer, and her résumé reads like a tour of Indian cinema's most visually ambitious decade. She dressed the Chola dynasty in Mani Ratnam's *Ponniyin Selvan*. She wrapped Ranveer Singh in those unforgettable silhouettes for *Rocky Aur Rani Kii Prem Kahaani*. She designed for *Dunki*, *Leo*, *Sanju*, *Shershaah*. Every frame she touches looks like it belongs in a museum — or on a mood board.

Dilip Shankar, a Delhi-based casting director, has spent years doing the unglamorous work of finding the right face for the right story. His credits span Mira Nair's *Monsoon Wedding*, Ang Lee's *Life of Pi*, and Pan Nalin's *Last Film Show* — India's official Oscar entry in 2023. Shankar represents a profession that Bollywood has historically undervalued, and the Academy just gave it a seat at the table.

The Diaspora Angle

Perhaps the most striking name for NRI audiences is Avneet Kaur — not the social media star, but the Head of Characters and Technical Animation at Walt Disney Animation Studios. She is, quite literally, one of the people who decides how Disney characters move, breathe, and feel on screen. For the Indian diaspora, her invitation isn't just recognition; it's a mirror. She's proof of what happens when Indian creative talent meets the machinery of Hollywood at the highest level.

Documentary filmmaker Shalini Kantayya also joins the class, along with production and technology professionals Farah Khan (not the *Om Shanti Om* director — a different Farah Khan working in production infrastructure) and Rajesh Ramachandran, plus visual effects artists who work across Indian and international productions.

What It Actually Means

Academy membership isn't honorary. It's functional. Every one of these invitees, if they accept, gets a vote in the Oscar nominations and final selections — including Best International Feature Film, where India has historically struggled to break through despite a staggering volume of world-class work.

The numbers tell their own story: 42% of this year's class are women. 56% belong to underrepresented communities. 53% come from 60 countries outside the United States. If all 529 accept, total Academy membership rises to 11,319. The body that once looked almost exclusively like old Hollywood is slowly, deliberately, starting to look like the world that watches its movies.

For Indian cinema, seven new voters may sound modest. But consider the arc. A decade ago, Indian representation in the Academy was negligible. Today, between this class and previous inductees — Aamir Khan, Guneet Monga, Nandita Das, Karan Johar, Anurag Kashyap, Priyanka Chopra Jonas, and others — the Indian voting bloc is becoming substantial enough to matter in tight races.

The 99th Academy Awards are scheduled for March 14, 2027, at the Dolby Theatre in Hollywood. When the envelopes are opened that night, the hands doing the choosing will include a few more that know exactly what a Bhardwaj score sounds like, what a Sreekar Prasad cut feels like, and what it means to dress a queen in a Lakhani costume.

Indian cinema didn't just get invited to the party. It got handed a ballot.
